newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Cyclone ravages Bangladesh, killing hundreds.
newsitem.headline: Cyclone ravages Bangladesh, killing hundreds.

text.p: More than 350 people were killed when a severe cyclone swept Bangladesh's flat coastal region on Monday, newspaper reporters in Chittagong said.
They said over 100 people died in the islands of Maheshkhali, Kutubdia and Saint Martin's. Some 250 were killed in Cox's Bazar.
Some 2,000 people were believed injured in Chittagong port city alone and about 100 fishermen from the coastal district of Patuakhali were missing at sea.
Official sources, hampered by the cutting of telephone links, confirmed only nine deaths and more than 100 injured in Chittagong, but said the figures could go up on Tuesday.
Chittagong journalists said however contacted local government agencies direct by radio to compile their casualty figures.
The cyclone, roaring in from the Bay of Bengal, ravaged Chittagong, Cox's Bazar and Tenkaf districts and several islands, leaving a trail of devastation.
"It's difficult to estimate losses of lives and property in the dark. All affected areas have been without electricity and many without telecommunications," one Chittagong official said.
Doctors at Chittagong Medical College Hospital also said they feared the death toll would rise as more reports came in.
"This was major devastation and we think many more casualties will follow," one said.
Officials in Chittagong said thousands of houses were demolished, and uprooted trees and power poles jammed roads. Power and communications were cut in many areas.
Two opposition legislators said more than 100,000 houses were damaged on the outskirts of Chittagong city alone.

Director-General of Police in Chittagong, Abdur Rahim, said: "Our men were busy trying to protect themselves. At least 50 policemen and 30 paramilitary guards were injured, mostly by flying debris, when more than ten barracks were blown down."
A border guard in Cox's Bazar told his headquarters by radio: "Village after village has been levelled by the cyclone. There have been many casualties but we cannot count them because of darkness."
The Panamanian-registered cargo ship Esco Argo sent an SOS message to storm-battered Chittagong port on Monday night, saying it was sinking near Kutubdia island, port officials said.

They said the ship, which arrived in Chittagong on Sunday from Bangkok carrying 3,235 tonnes of cement, had been sent to an outer anchorage for safety before the 200 kph (124 mph) cyclone struck on Monday afternoon.
The Bangladeshi ship the Pioneer and survey vessel Anusandhani might also have sunk, one port official said. Another Bangladeshi freighter, the Q.C. Teal, broke anchor and was drifting at sea.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina cancelled a trip abroad and said she hoped Bangladeshis would face the crisis with courage. She assured them there would be no shortage of relief materials.
More than 100 medical teams were on standby to help victims. Army, navy, paramilitary guards and police had been called in to help.
"Many houses have been destroyed and we can see sheets of tin from rooftops flying like tree leaves," Cox's Bazar district administrator Ali Imam Majumder told Reuters.
Weather officials said they feared the cyclone could trigger a tidal surge of up to five metres (15 ft), inundating huge areas.

Saint Martin's island near Teknaf was under two metres (six feet) of water. Several other islands had been battered by the cyclone and could be inundated, Red Crescent said quoting their field volunteers.
Bangladesh's worst cyclone in 1991 killed at least 138,000 people and left millions homeless.

"Damage from the latest cyclone could be more than in 1991," said Sajedur Rahman, director of Dhaka's Meterology office. "But casualties are expected to be much lower (than 1991) because we had enough time to warn, alert and evacuate people."
Information ministry officials said one million people had been evacuated from the cyclone's path by more than 33,000 Red Crescent and other volunteers.
Fishermen had been warned not to leave port. Dozens of ships berthed at Chittagong and Mongla ports were moved to outer anchorages, port officials said.
Weather officials said the storm started losing strength immediately after it swept past Chittagong.

State-run radio and television earlier asked people fleeing their homes or being moved to cyclone shelters to store drinking water, food and other essentials underground to help them after the cyclone passed.
